title: Desert hiker with headache and swollen fingers after heavy water intake

source.title: Case Study: Is Hydration Always the Answer?

classification.acuity_basis: No altered mental status; improved with fluid restriction and salt; evacuated by ATV same day.

context.terrain: sandy wash, one small juniper for shade
context.distance_to_care: unknown; nearest water 2 h round trip; dirt road nearby

presentation.summary: Fit hiker becomes unusually tired, dizzy and headachy in desert heat. Companion says they are slower to respond than usual. Fingers are swollen for the first time ever.
exam_findings: slightly slow to respond per companion
presentation.last_intake_output: 8 L plain water yesterday; 4 L today plus 1 L in last hour; one bagel; one urination today; clear urine
presentation.events_leading_up: 8 mi yesterday, 5 mi today, hiking mornings/evenings; sun hat and loose white shirt

assessment: heat stroke unlikely for now (temp, no clear altered mental status)
heat exhaustion/dehydration possible but no thirst, clear urine, large intake argue against
overhydration / hyponatremia possible: large intake, little food, swollen fingers; likely mild-moderate
plan: move off hot ground to shade on a pad, sponge with water
send team for water and team to ridge for cell signal
restrict water, give salty snacks, monitor mental status and temperature
anticipated_problems: no improvement and continued inability to travel
teaching_points: Core temp >40C with altered mental status suggests heat stroke.
Hyponatremia is easily mistaken for dehydration/heat exhaustion; giving fluids makes it worse.
Wrongly pushing fluids for overhydration is more dangerous than briefly delaying fluids for dehydration when no immediate life threat exists.
Treat suspected mild-moderate hyponatremia with fluid restriction, salty food, and waiting for urination; concentrated salty broth can help but may cause nausea.

decision_points.question: Give more water?
decision_points.source_decision: No; restrict fluids and give salt

outcome.summary: Began urinating heavily, weak but standing in a few hours; later thirsty, drank salted water; walked to dirt road and got an ATV ride to town.

must_ask: how much water have you drunk today and yesterday?
when did you last pee and what color?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate promptly if confusion, vomiting, seizure or worsening mental status.
must_not_recommend: hydrate aggressively without a fluid history

lay_queries: I've been drinking tons of water but feel dizzy and have a headache
my fingers are swollen and I feel awful in the heat
should I drink more water heat headache

title: Trail runner feeling awful after drinking 6 L in 4 hours

classification.acuity_basis: Normal mental status; improved with rest and fluid restriction; walked out.

context.distance_to_care: 4 mi to trailhead; ATV or helicopter accessible

pertinent_history: history of bonking in long efforts

presentation.summary: Twenty miles into a hot trail run, a runner says he feels awful: dizzy, shaky, nauseated, anxious with a dull headache. He has drained his 2 L pack twice plus more and hasn't urinated since starting.
presentation.last_intake_output: ~6 L water since 06:00; 2 energy bars (200 mg Na each) + 1 salt tab (215 mg); no urination since start

plan: monitor; evacuation premature given distance and daylight
teaching_points: Main risk factor for exertional hyponatremia is excess fluid, e.g. >1-1.5 L/h for several hours.
Salt tablets do not prevent hyponatremia if overdrinking.
Drink to thirst.
Field care: slow/stop fluids until symptoms resolve and give salty snacks; snacks alone won't fix it.
Neurologic signs or altered mental status require prompt evacuation.

outcome.summary: After an hour he urinated a large volume of clear urine, symptoms eased except headache; walked out tired.

must_recognize: hyponatremia vs heat exhaustion vs hypoglycemia
must_ask: how much have you drunk since starting?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate promptly for confusion, persistent vomiting or seizure.
must_not_recommend: drink more water to fix it
salt tablets as prevention while overdrinking

lay_queries: feel dizzy and shaky on a long run even though I've been drinking a lot
haven't peed all run but drank 6 liters
red_flags: nausea and headache with heavy drinking

title: Frozen fingertips on a backcountry ski trip: thaw or not?

source.title: Case Study: How to Manage Frostbite

classification.acuity_basis: Frostbite thawed in camp; skied out next day for care.

context.weather: highs -12C, lows -28C; next day forecast below -17C

presentation.summary: At camp, a skier who struggled to keep hands warm has white, numb, firm distal right fingertips; rest of the hand cool, pale and soft. Not hypothermic.
presentation.chief_complaint: possible frostbite right fingers (noticed by companion)
exam_findings: distal right finger joints white, numb, firm
rest of hand cool, pale, soft

plan: decide whether to thaw in the field
anticipated_problems: thawed fingers must stay warm and protected on ski-out; very cold forecast
teaching_points: Warm water bath rapid thaw is ideal.
Injury worsens the longer tissue stays frozen.
Refreezing after thaw causes much worse injury; only thaw if you can keep it thawed.
Thawing is painful and thawed tissue is fragile and unusable.
Remove rings and bracelets before thawing.

decision_points.question: Thaw in the field?
decision_points.source_decision: Yes, in warm water bath in camp
basis: can keep tissue warm overnight and during ski out

outcome.summary: 15 min bath (patient's tolerance); fingers pink; clear blisters by morning; pain 7/10; fingers padded and mitted, skied out 4 h without pole. Lost fingernails only.

must_ask: can you keep the hand warm after thawing until you reach help?
is the tissue hard or soft?
eval.must_escalate: Arrange evacuation after thaw for frostbite with blisters.
must_not_recommend: thawing near a fire or stove

lay_queries: my fingertips are white and hard and I can't feel them
should I warm up frostbitten fingers in the tent

title: Lost hunter found after 36 hours: severe hypothermia and frostbite

source.title: Case Study 33: Lost in a Snowstorm

classification.acuity_basis: Responsive to pain only, HR 30, RR 6; arrested in ED.

context.weather: 2 days wet snowstorm then clear; dawn -18C; knee-deep snow
context.distance_to_care: ~60 min ground to EMS; no air available; ED 2.5 h after found

presentation.summary: Hunter missing two nights is found face-down after falling into an unfrozen creek. Responds only to pain with a moan; no palpable pulse; very slow heart and breathing on auscultation.
presentation.chief_complaint: unable to give (responds to pain only)
exam_findings: white waxy hard tissue on all fingers, toes/forefeet, nose, ears, 8 in patch left upper abdomen
pertinent_negatives: no other injuries except small leg bruises

assessment: partial and full thickness frostbite fingers, toes, nose, ears, abdomen
plan: dry, in sleeping bag inside two more bags and plastic sheet
slow, gentle vehicle transport to ALS rendezvous
do not treat frostbite in the field
anticipated_problems: cardiac arrest from cold-induced cardiac instability
teaching_points: Mild hypothermia: keep dry, insulated, out of wind, give calories to fuel shivering; exercise only for alert walking patients.
Severe hypothermia: goal is stabilization and transport, not field rewarming.
Handle gently and keep horizontal; rough or upright movement linked to post-rescue collapse.
Wrapped heat sources to chest and armpits; avoid walking or exercise.
Do not start compressions unless pulselessness is confirmed (check carefully); CPR may continue well beyond 30 min in hypothermia.

outcome.summary: Arrived ED at ~23.9C still breathing; then arrested; 3 h CPR with active rewarming; defibrillated successfully; survived with extensive frostbite tissue loss.
outcome.final_diagnosis: severe hypothermia with cardiac arrest, extensive frostbite

must_recognize: severe hypothermia (reduced responsiveness, very slow pulse/breathing)
must_ask: check pulse and breathing for a full minute
must_not_recommend: starting CPR on a patient with a slow pulse
giving food or drink to an unresponsive person

lay_queries: found someone in the snow barely breathing and ice cold
can't find a pulse he's frozen
should I do CPR on a frozen person

title: Hiker knocked down by nearby lightning strike above treeline

source.title: Case Study: Hiking through a Thunderstorm

classification.acuity_basis: No lightning injury signs; abrasions and bruise; trip continued with monitoring.

context.terrain: alpine meadow below 11,600 ft pass, 2 mi to forest

presentation.summary: Pushing across open alpine terrain in a storm, a hiker falls when lightning strikes close by, is briefly stunned, then walks half a mile to treeline.
presentation.chief_complaint: left shoulder, hip and knee pain
exam_findings: muddy abrasions left knee and hip
mild left shoulder swelling, full ROM

assessment: dirty abrasions left knee and hip
teaching_points: Thunder audible means move to safer terrain early.
No outdoor place is safe; avoid summits, ridges, open terrain, isolated trees, water, shallow caves/overhangs.
Flash-to-bang distance is unreliable in mountains (~5 s per mile / 3 s per km).
Last resort: spread group within voice contact and use lightning position on a pad, feet together.

outcome.summary: Wounds cleaned and dressed; trip continued.
outcome.final_diagnosis: shoulder contusion, abrasions; no lightning injury

must_recognize: possible lightning injury needs check of consciousness, burns, hearing, vision, heart
must_ask: can they hear and see normally?
any chest pain or irregular heartbeat?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if loss of consciousness, burns, neuro or cardiac symptoms.
must_not_recommend: huddling the group together in the open

lay_queries: lightning hit right next to us and my friend fell down
we're above treeline and there's lightning what do we do

title: Fatigued backpacker at altitude with cough and low oxygen: HAPE

source.title: Case Study: Finding a Sick Person High in the Mountains

classification.acuity_basis: SpO2 74%, rales; HAPE causes most altitude deaths; helicopter evacuation.

presentation.summary: SAR finds a weak, fatigued backpacker sitting on a log 8 miles in. Several days of heavy cough thought to be flu, then headache, nausea, no appetite and lethargy. Walked only 4 miles in 8 hours downhill with a light pack.
presentation.events_leading_up: Day1 drove 900 m to 2400 m; Day2 hiked to 3100 m; Day3 to 3200 m, symptoms began; Day4 rested no better; Day5 descending, weaker

plan: move downhill on oxygen 1/4 mi to meadow LZ
oxygen 4 L/min nasal cannula; request more
teaching_points: Risk factors: fast ascent, overexertion, sleeping higher than acclimatized; fitness doesn't protect.
AMS: headache, anorexia, nausea, dizziness, insomnia, fatigue; stop ascent, descend if no improvement.
HACE: ataxia and altered mental status; immediate descent.
HAPE: reduced exercise tolerance, breathlessness, unexpected fatigue, rising HR/RR, cough; cyanosis or wet lung sounds are danger signs; descend and give oxygen.
Exertion worsens HAPE.

outcome.summary: Walked slowly on oxygen to LZ; flown to hospital; admitted overnight, released when lungs cleared.

must_recognize: HAPE: fatigue + cough + breathlessness after ascent
must_ask: how fast did you climb and where did you sleep?
eval.must_escalate: Descend immediately and evacuate; oxygen if available.
must_not_recommend: resting at the same altitude to see if it improves when HAPE suspected

lay_queries: I'm at altitude and so tired I can barely walk and coughing a lot
friend has a bad cough and is exhausted in the mountains
is it flu or altitude sickness

title: Snowshoe course student with numb pale toes

classification.acuity_basis: Big toe remained purple and cold after thaw; snowmobile evac to hospital.

pertinent_history: previous episodes of cold painful toes

presentation.summary: After a 3-mile snowshoe and sweaty shelter digging, a student reports toes cold and numb all day. All ten toes pale and cold; left big toe hard.
exam_findings: left big toe cold, pale, hard; others soft
good pedal pulse, can move toes

assessment: possible local cold injury to toes
plan: evacuate if frostbite evident after warming
teaching_points: You can't judge extent until tissue is warm.
Ideal thaw: water bath 37-39C; avoid fire, hot air, rubbing.
Thawed tissue must not refreeze.
After warming, swelling, persistent numbness, gray/purple color, or blisters suggest frostbite and warrant evacuation.
Walking on frozen feet can worsen injury.

decision_points.question: Evacuate after rewarming?
basis: left big toe dark purple and cold after rewarming

outcome.summary: Rewarmed on instructor's abdomen 15-20 min; one toe stayed purple; SAR snowmobile to road and hospital; lost tip of big toe and nail.

must_ask: is the skin hard or soft?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if discoloration, persistent numbness or blisters after rewarming.
must_not_recommend: walking on frozen feet if avoidable

lay_queries: my toes are numb and white after snowshoeing
one toe is still purple after warming it up
